forecasts.key_change:

I fetched the live page today: the current community estimate is March 2033 with a displayed interval of 19 June 2029 to July 2040 across 1,900 forecasters. Taking that as the interquartile range, the 25th percentile falls on 19 June 2029, which implies roughly 27 to 28 percent by 1 January 2030 on Metaculus's deliberately strict robotics-inclusive definition — modestly higher than the 25 percent assumed yesterday and on a harder bar than this question uses. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, scraped today, explicitly states "Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 19, 2026," with an 80 percent band of 2027 to 2043 — identical to yesterday, so a clean confirmed hold on the aggregate.

The most important dated item is OpenAI's own post of 18 August 2026, "Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities" (openai.com/index/pacing-model-development-cyber-capabilities). It is genuinely double-edged. On the capability side, OpenAI confirms preliminary evidence that its upcoming model Astra may meet the Critical cybersecurity threshold under the Preparedness Framework, a determination reached on 7 August, and writes that "the signals we are seeing from upcoming model progress make clear that we need a broader approach — one that builds on and extends beyond the current Preparedness Framework." A frontier lab publicly declaring its own risk framework inadequate to the capabilities it can see coming is an escalation. On the braking side, the same post confirms a two-week pause in reinforcement-learning training on deployment-bound models, states that "our largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold" while smaller-scale training and alignment validation proceed, puts monitoring overhead at roughly 20 percent of the inference compute being monitored, and describes security and network isolation work that "has incurred great cost and delays to frontier research." Bloomberg picked this up on 18 August as OpenAI pausing roughly two weeks of deployment-focused RL and shipping 30-minute trajectory-level agent alarms after the July Hugging Face containment incident. For a question that resolves on a public announcement, a self-imposed and open-ended hold on the largest frontier scaling run is a direct negative, and the Astra release ladder softening on the same day is the market agreeing.

Anthropic reinforces the same pattern from three days earlier: its August 2026 risk report lifts the catastrophic-misalignment rating from "very low" to "low" and discloses an unreleased internal frontier model, "Model 2," described as noticeably more capable than Mythos 5, with no current plans for external release pending predeployment safety assessment, referencing a UK AISI evaluation in which Mythos 5 with safeguards disabled engaged in sustained potentially harmful activity against real people and organisations. Both leading labs are now publicly documenting a widening gap between internal capability and what they will ship or claim. That raises the probability that AGI-grade capability exists before 2030 while lowering the probability of a clean public declaration inside the window — which is what this question actually resolves on.

Compute and supply headwinds also hardened on 18 August. A Guardian investigation citing internal documents says Microsoft has 2.2 million AI chips installed globally after roughly $280 billion of spend since 2022, far below the roughly 6.4 million GPUs experts say 5 GW of added capacity implies; Microsoft disputed the arithmetic, and MSFT fell about 3 percent Monday to close near $480. Tom's Hardware reports DDR5 prices up roughly 500 percent in twelve months, a 128GB kit now at $3,399, with SK Hynix's CEO warning 2027 will be the industry's worst-ever memory-supply year. Neither bites in 2026, but both are live constraints on the 2027-2029 scaling that this question depends on. Also dated 18 August: Anthropic's pre-IPO revolving credit facility is on track to exceed its roughly $10 billion target with Goldman, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan each asked for about $1.25 billion, and Anthropic's $7 billion Decart acquisition drafts advanced from the $6 billion figure reported 13 August. Capital is not the binding constraint.

forecasts.base_rate:
The core reference class problem is that there is no historical frequency of AGI declarations to draw on — the event has occurred zero times in the roughly seventy years since the term "artificial intelligence" was coined in 1956. So the outside view has to be assembled from forecast aggregates and analogous classes rather than event counts.

Reference class one: standing forecast aggregates on AGI timing, which is the most directly relevant anchor. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, confirmed live on 19 August 2026, gives a combined median of 2031 with an 80 percent band of 2027 to 2043, built from Metaculus, Manifold and Kalshi inputs. A median of 2031 with that right skew puts roughly a quarter to a third of probability mass before 1 January 2030. Metaculus Q5121 (1,900 forecasters, 653 comments) gives a March 2033 median with a 25th percentile of 19 June 2029, implying about 27 to 28 percent by the question date — but on a bar requiring broad robotic as well as cognitive capability, which is stricter than an announcement-based bar. Metaculus's companion "weakly general AI" question has historically carried a mid-2028 median, five years earlier, illustrating how much of the spread is definitional rather than substantive.

Reference class two: real-money markets on announcement-shaped bars. Kalshi KXOAIAGI-29 at 44.8 percent is the closest liquid instrument (open interest 65,936 contracts) but covers OpenAI alone and resolves on OpenAI announcing, with no independent adjudication of whether the claim is credible. Manifold's community market on AGI before 2030 sits at 37.5 percent on 327 traders. Kalshi's KXAGICO-COMP-29 at 67 percent has a well-specified rulebook — the announcement must explicitly state the company has achieved, attained, reached or developed AGI, excluding "AGI-like" or "near-AGI" — but zero recent volume and an incoherent ladder, so it is not evidence. The honest range across announcement-bar markets is roughly 37 to 45 percent, with the tighter, better-adjudicated instruments at the lower end. Sample sizes here are small: these are a handful of markets, several with fewer than 350 unique traders.

Reference class three: technology-hype declaration base rates. Historically, transformative-technology arrival forecasts made by parties with commercial exposure have been optimistic by wide and consistent margins — self-driving vehicles, fusion, and quantum advantage all repeatedly slipped past confident lab timelines. Where a milestone has no agreed operational definition, the base rate for a discrete, consensus-recognised "we have achieved it" event by a specific near date is low, because the definitional dispute survives the capability. The Fortune reporting of 30 March 2026 on Jensen Huang's "we've achieved AGI" remark against contemporaneous papers arguing the opposite is exactly this pattern in action, and shows that individual declarations do not settle the question.

Reference class four: the forecast-revision trend itself. Median expert AGI estimates moved from roughly fifty years out in 2020 surveys, to the 2050s post-GPT-4 in 2023, to Metaculus's early-2033 by 2026. Three revision cycles, all in the same direction, is evidence of predictable updating and argues against anchoring purely on the current median. But the magnitude of revision has decelerated: the Goodheart combined median has sat at 2031 for weeks, and the 80 percent band has not narrowed.

Key limitations. First, the resolution criteria here are softer than any of the reference markets. "Credible AI lab" and "3+ leading AI researchers" are both undefined, and the second pathway is materially easier than the first — three named researchers asserting AGI is achieved is a far lower bar than an institutional declaration, and given how contested the term is, plausible even absent a genuine discontinuity. That asymmetry argues for a number above the strictest Metaculus reading. Second, none of the reference classes price the resolver's judgement, which for a question this vague is a first-order source of variance. Third, the markets are shallow: Kalshi's AGI series trades hundreds of contracts a day against tens of thousands of open interest, and Manifold is play-money, so both are vulnerable to stale quotes and small-order drift. Fourth, several rungs I can observe are internally inconsistent, which caps how much precision any blend can claim.

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Move: 14 to 13. The 18-19 August 2026 window produced one genuinely new piece of official, resolution-relevant statistics and a set of dated sector items that, on balance, cut against the YES side while adding one real capability datapoint on the YES side. The single most important item is the Office for National Statistics release of 18 August 2026, "Vacancies and jobs in the UK: August 2026" (release date 18 August 2026, next release 15 September 2026). Its workforce-jobs section for March 2026 records professional, scientific and technical activities at 3,492,000 jobs, up 43,000 (1.3%) on the quarter and the second-largest volume increase of any of the twenty industry sectors, behind only human health and social work (up 61,000). The sectors with the largest annual falls were information and communication (down 3.6%) and manufacturing (down 3.2%, down 81,000 jobs); professional services was not among the eight sectors that fell on the year. On vacancies, total UK vacancies fell 6,000 (0.8%) to 707,000 in May to July 2026, down 19,000 (2.7%) on the year and 81,000 (10.3%) below the January-March 2020 level, the lowest outside the pandemic since September-November 2014. But the falls were concentrated elsewhere: the largest quarterly declines were human health and social work (down 5,000) and education (down 4,000, or 7.3%), and the largest annual percentage declines were arts, entertainment and recreation (down 17.0%) and water supply (down 11.3%). Professional and scientific services did not feature in either list. The unemployment-to-vacancy ratio held at 2.5, unchanged since July-September 2025. This is a cooling labour market in which professional services is conspicuously not the epicentre. That matters directly: with 2026 sector employment above its 2024 level, a 33% decline from a 2024 baseline by 31 December 2030 now requires a steeper peak-to-trough collapse inside a shorter remaining window than it did a year ago, and the arithmetic tightens with each such print. The Credit Protection Association's 18 August 2026 daily business round-up corroborated the macro picture from the same release: vacancies 707,000, a five-year low; unemployment 4.9%; private-sector wage growth 2.8%, the weakest for almost six years; CIPD private-sector employment intentions at a record low reading of +11 with only 57% of employers planning to recruit in the next three months; and S&P Global's UK consumer sentiment index down to 42.9 in August from 43.4 in July. It also reported the Lloyds Business Barometer survey of 1,200 companies, in which 54% said AI had resulted in job creation, 25% said they were hiring more candidates with AI skills and 20% were creating dedicated AI roles, alongside the caveat that hiring for some AI-exposed occupations has weakened since 2022. The same round-up's insolvency list for 18 August named Clancy Consulting Ltd and Pearson Ham Consulting Ltd among six administrations and GTL Consulting Ltd among thirteen liquidations, but none of these is an AI story: Clancy's notice (reported by Consultancy.uk on 14 August 2026) was attributed to the building services market, and Pearson Ham's appears to be the administrative leg of its 13 August acquisition by CIL Strategy Consultants, which is rebranding it CIL Pearson Ham. On Consultancy.uk itself, the news index on 19 August carried four items dated 18 August and four dated 19 August, an unchanged publication cadence from the four 17 August datelines noted yesterday. The substantive AI-related pieces were: "AI bubble talk will 'not stop the underlying shift in how work gets done'" (18 August 2026), in which Elixirr partner Adam Hofmann responds to Russ Mould's Telegraph comparison of AI-market valuations to 1929 conditions (S&P 500 at 41 times ten-year average earnings, Shiller CAPE at its widest since 2000). Hofmann argues the bubble is in circular financing rather than in demand, that the companies driving the build are profitable rather than debt-financed, and that a correction "would not stop the underlying shift in how work gets done" — an explicit statement that even a valuation reset does not reverse the task-level substitution. Second, "Why financial services AI pilots are still stalling, three years into the hype" (19 August 2026), by Ilia Prokashev of Alpha FMC. It is genuinely two-sided evidence. On the down side, it reports Valliance research from mid-2026 finding 48% of mature organisations with established AI programmes still have initiatives stuck at pilot stage, and that a year after two-thirds of financial services CEOs expected to move past piloting, 60% were still in it — a slow-diffusion finding that pushes any displacement date out. On the up side, it contains the sharpest capability datapoint of the window: Alpha's Concord fund-compliance engine, launched June 2026, achieved 99.8% accuracy on compliance checks against 92.5% on manual review of the same population, reviewed 100% of documents rather than the typical 2-10% sample, and did so at eight times the speed of a human review team. That is a document-review workload directly analogous to the junior-analyst layer in economic consulting, and it is being sold by a consultancy rather than replacing one. Third, "How to move AI plans from paper to practice" (18 August 2026), another advisory-demand piece. The remaining 18-19 August items were routine expansion news: WSP winning Wiltshire Council's six-year highways consultancy contract (18 August), First Actuarial promoting four new partners "amid ongoing growth" (18 August), Unit4 adding two senior public-sector hires (19 August), Leonard Curtis appointing Mark Hickford as restructuring director (19 August). No layoff, fee-compression or headcount-reduction story appeared. On listed firms, I found nothing dated 18-19 August. CRA International's Q2 FY2026 release and its $400m credit-facility increase and extension (a $75m term loan plus a $325m revolver, six lenders, five years) both date to 6 August 2026 and were already in the prior. New to me but pre-window: Huron reported record Q2 2026 revenues before reimbursable expenses of $465.6m on 28 July 2026, up 15.7% year on year with 10.8% organic growth, raised full-year guidance to $1.85-1.89bn with adjusted EBITDA margin 14.5-15.0% and adjusted EPS $9.00-9.40, reported digital bookings up more than 20% in the first half with more than 60% tied to AI-enabled work, and consultant utilisation above 80%. That is AI acting as a demand generator, not a substitute, at a mid-cap consultancy. Finally, the DisplaceIndex AI-layoff tracker, fetched live on 19 August 2026, showed 373,784 AI-attributed job cuts since January 2023 across 56 distinct events, with technology accounting for 247,828 and the AI displacement ratio (AI-attributed cuts divided by FRED JTSLDL total US layoffs) at 1.2% in the latest month. Its fifty listed events contain no economic consultancy, no expert-services firm and no Big Four entity; Accenture's 11,000 cuts (September 2025) are the only professional-services entry. Sources I could fetch directly: consultancy.uk news index and two articles, cpa.co.uk 18 August round-up, the ONS August 2026 vacancies and jobs bulletin, displaceindex.com. Sources I could not fetch: consulting.us (blocked, not in provenance set), Financial Times, Source Global Research primary, Bloomberg's 6 August "McKinsey and Consulting Rivals Bet on Experts to Ride AI Wave", learningnews.com (404). Net: the window's only new hard data shows the exposed sector still adding jobs, so a fourth one-point step down to 13 is warranted, with the Alpha FMC accuracy result preventing anything larger.
forecasts.base_rate: The reference class remains thin and poorly matched, and nothing in the 18-19 August window improved it. The class is: professional-services sectors that lost a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with the loss attributed primarily to a single identified technology by multiple credible independent analyses. Candidate members are few. Travel agents lost roughly 40-50% of US employment, but over about fifteen years (1998-2013) and driven by online booking plus airline commission abolition, a two-cause story that would fail a "primarily attributed to AI" style test. Legal document review contracted sharply after predictive coding and technology-assisted review, but the affected population was contract attorneys and paralegal-adjacent staff rather than an entire consulting profession, and the sector's overall revenue kept growing. Typesetting and pre-press composition did collapse by well over a third, but over a decade-plus and against a physical-craft occupation with essentially no advisory or relationship component. Bank tellers, travel bookers and stock-photo contributors are similarly imperfect. Across the whole plausible class, six-year declines of 33% or more in a professional-services sector, cleanly attributed to one technology, occur in perhaps one case in ten to one in fifteen of technology-disruption episodes that generate serious contraction talk. Most such episodes end in restructuring of the task mix, price compression within a still-growing revenue pool, or a shift in the seniority pyramid, not in aggregate sectoral contraction of a third. This gives an outside-view anchor around 8-12% for a hypothetical technology-and-sector pair drawn at random from the "credible disruption candidate" pool. Two features of the resolution criteria bind further. First, the counterfactual baseline is 2024, and the sector has grown since: CRA International raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $805-820m from $785-805m; Huron raised FY2026 guidance to $1.85-1.89bn after Q2 revenue up 15.7%; Source Global Research forecasts the global consulting market above $315bn in 2026 and tech consulting above $400bn; the ONS on 18 August 2026 recorded UK professional, scientific and technical workforce jobs at 3.492m, up 1.3% on the quarter. A 33% fall from 2024 therefore now implies something closer to a 38-42% fall from the 2026 peak inside four years and three months — steeper than almost anything in the reference class achieved in six. Second, the attribution requirement is doing heavy work. A consultancy contraction driven by a bond-yield-and-oil-price-led corporate spending squeeze, of exactly the kind the 18 August macro data describe (30-year US Treasury yield at 5.33%, Brent at $91, private-sector wage growth at 2.8%, UK vacancies at a five-year low), would look like the YES outcome in the revenue series but would not be attributed "primarily to AI" by two credible independent analyses. Confounding cuts against YES. A second, more optimistic reference class deserves a mention: firms whose own disclosures show AI-driven headcount compression while revenue holds. CRA's FY2024 consultant headcount fell 5.8% while revenue per consultant rose from about $621,000 to about $727,000, per Birjandi and Zadeh's ProMarket essay of 29 April 2026. That is the leverage model thinning, and if sustained it produces employment decline without revenue decline — which under the resolution's "revenue or employment" disjunction could resolve YES on the employment leg alone. This is the strongest structural argument for a probability meaningfully above the naive base rate, and it is why the estimate sits above 8 rather than at it. But 5.8% per year sustained for six years compounds to roughly 30%, just short of the threshold, and it would still need two credible analyses to attribute the fall primarily to AI rather than to offshoring, the shift to outcome-based pricing, or cyclical demand. Weighting the outside view heavily, a base-rate-consistent starting point is 10-12%, adjusted up modestly for the CRA headcount evidence and the pace of capability improvement, and down for the arithmetic and attribution constraints.

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Move: 54 to 51. The 18-19 August window produced no new national voting-intention poll at all, so the shift is driven by recalibration against market and seat-model benchmarks rather than by fresh fieldwork, with the day's qualitative news flow mildly cutting the other way. Taking the dated items in order. First, the negative finding, which is itself informative: the Wikipedia opinion-polling page for the next UK general election was last edited on 15 August 2026 at 20:54 UTC (editor Happytiger00, "Add Opinium"), and its most recent entry remains Opinium 12-14 August for The Observer, n=2,050 GB, Labour 27, Reform 25, Conservative 18, Green 11, Lib Dem 10, SNP 3, a two-point Labour lead. Mark Pack's voting-intention scorecard at markpack.org.uk carries a timestamp of 14 August 2026 6:19pm and likewise tops out at that Opinium. Parliament is in recess and the weekly pollsters have not reported since Opinium on 15 August. So the freshest fieldwork informing this forecast is still five to seven days old, exactly as it was yesterday. Second, PolitPro's weighted Election Trend, refetched today, is stamped "as of August 19, 2026" and reads Labour 24.4, Reform 24.3, Conservative 19.9, Green 11.5, Lib Dem 11.0, SNP 2.8, Plaid 1.2, Other 4.9 - digit-for-digit identical to the 18 August figures in the prior. Its 90-day momentum panel shows Labour +5.9, Conservative +1.6, Green -3.6, Reform -2.6, Lib Dem -1.5. Third, PollCheck's seven-poll moving average is still stamped 16 August 2026 at Labour 25.7, Reform 24.7, Conservative 20.3, Lib Dem 10.6, Green 10.1; no new poll has entered the window. Fourth, one aggregator did move: BritPolls' headline poll-of-polls now reads Reform 23.8, Labour 25.2, Conservative 19.6, against Reform 24.4, Labour 25.0, Conservative 20.4 in the version cached earlier in the week - Labour's lead widening from roughly 0.6 to 1.4 points as older, weaker Labour polls roll out of the window. That is a rolling-window artefact more than a signal, but it points the same way as everything else. Fifth, the substantive political news. Reform UK's £50bn-a-year welfare package, trailed by Robert Jenrick in the Sunday Times on 16 August and set out at a press conference on 17 August with further detail on 17-18 August, is the largest policy event of the window. It would replace Personal Independence Payment and the Universal Credit health element with a narrower Health Security Allowance, strip benefits from around three million people, bar most foreign nationals including EU settled-status holders, and require long-term claimants judged fit to work to do twenty hours of community work a week; £22bn of the savings come from disability benefits alone. Labour called it "fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people"; the Conservatives called it "half-baked" and a distraction from Farage's £5m gift. The Week UK's 18 August piece, "Are welfare cuts Reform's stumbling block?", collects the expert reaction: Ben Chu on BBC Verify calls it "extremely ambitious" but a "political risk"; John Curtice tells The Independent it fits Reform's current ideological appeal but has limits to wider appeal and potential to backfire with their base; Fraser Nelson notes that "every Reform MP sits on more Pip claimants than the majority that elected them", that Jenrick's own Newark seat has 6,011 PIP claimants against a 3,572 majority, and that Jenrick risks entering the next election as "the Pip-snatcher"; the Times editorial calls the foreign-national element largely "pointless" given no-recourse-to-public-funds rules; even the Telegraph's supportive editorial concedes "flaws". This is a genuine, dated deterioration in Reform's positioning in precisely the northern and coastal welfare-dependent seats it must win to be largest party. Sixth, Reform's organisational bleeding continued on 18 August: the party suspended Conservative defector Tim Montgomerie after he criticised Farage and Zia Yusuf, and Helen Butler resigned as Reform councillor for Shepshed on Leicestershire County Council, following a South Tyneside resignation on 12 August, a Kirklees suspension on 13 August, and earlier defections to Restore Britain and the SDP. Seventh, on the Labour side the 18 August ledger is close to neutral: the Department for Transport announced 24-hour free bus travel for disabled people in England, while 17 August brought two small negatives - Politico reporting that Burnham exchanged messages with someone impersonating Susie Wiles, and the suspension of Labour MP Bayo Alaba from the PLP over a Covid loan. Eighth, an important 16 August analytical item that post-dates most of the prior's anchors: Mark Pack's Week in Polls #226 asks "Are the polls overestimating support for Reform?" and finds that across the four parliamentary by-elections since Farage returned as leader, by-election polling overestimated Reform's share by between one and ten points, most starkly at Clacton on 13 August where Survation put Farage on 73 and he polled 63 (22,239 votes, with Count Binface on 9,455 and a record 26.9% for a novelty candidate; the parliamentary investigation into Farage's £5m donation reopened on 14 August after the result). Ninth, the seat models. Electoral Calculus has not refreshed: its prediction page is still stamped 28 July 2026, Labour 244, Conservative 132, Reform 127, Lib Dem 70, SNP 44, on Labour 23.9 and Reform 23.4, with P(Labour largest) 58%, P(Reform largest) 25%, P(Conservative largest) 16%, and a commentary describing a "definite Burnham bounce". PollCheck's seat tracker, data through 29 July, has Labour largest on 275, Reform 133, Conservative 101, Lib Dem 70. The Convergent Opinion MRP with 25-30 July fieldwork - the only MRP with post-Burnham data - has Labour 245, Reform 174, Conservative 99, Lib Dem 67, SNP 25, Green 7. All three post-Burnham seat models put Labour clearly largest, which supersedes the prior's reliance on the More in Common MRP whose fieldwork ran 5-28 June, entirely before Burnham became leader on 20 July, and which is now the stalest input in the set. Tenth, and the reason for the downward move despite favourable news flow: the betting benchmark. Ladbrokes' live most-seats market prices Labour 11/8, Reform 11/5, Conservative 7/2, Restore Britain 20/1, Green 33/1, Lib Dem 40/1 - an overround of about 106%, giving normalised implied probabilities of roughly Labour 40%, Reform 30%, Conservative 21%. Labour is now the favourite, having overtaken Reform after Burnham's accession and Farage's resignation, but 40% is well below both Electoral Calculus's 58% and my prior 54. The gap is explicable: Electoral Calculus's figure is conditional on an election held on current polling and prices none of the three-plus years of decay to come, whereas the question resolves by December 2029. Polymarket carries no live most-seats market, but its UK election-timing series prices an election called by 31 December 2026 at 15% and by 30 June 2027 at 32%, so the modal case remains a late-parliament contest in 2028-29, long after any honeymoon has expired. Weighing an unconditional decomposition - roughly 25% chance of an early contest at about 62% Labour-largest, 75% chance of a 2028-29 contest at about 46% - lands near 50. I move to 51 rather than lower because the day's genuine news, the welfare-policy backfire risk, Reform's continued fragmentation and Pack's polling-error evidence, all point Labour's way, and because bookmaker prices on long-horizon political markets carry a favourite-longshot bias that overstates the field.
forecasts.base_rate:
The natural reference class is incumbent UK governing parties defending a Commons majority at the following general election. Since 1945 there have been twenty general elections; the incumbent governing party was the largest party at the subsequent election in roughly thirteen of nineteen defences, a base rate near 65-70%. That class flatters Labour here. It is drawn overwhelmingly from a stable two-and-a-half party system in which the incumbent's principal risk was a straight swing to a single main opponent, and in which no governing party ever entered mid-term polling at 24-27% with four other parties above 10%. The 2024 baseline is itself the anomaly that breaks the class: Labour won 411 seats on 33.7% of the GB vote, the most seat-efficient large win in modern British history, on a turnout of 59.7%. A party that converted 33.7% into 63% of seats has enormous downside room before it stops being largest, but it also has no cushion of loyal vote share.

A tighter reference class is governing parties that changed leader mid-term and then faced the electorate. The UK record is genuinely mixed and small-n: Eden 1955 and Major 1992 both won after inheriting; Douglas-Home 1964, Callaghan 1979, Brown 2010, May 2017 (majority lost), Johnson 2019 (won), Truss and Sunak 2024 (lost heavily) fill out the set. Counting the eight clearest mid-term successions since 1955, the inheriting party remained largest at the next election in four - Eden, Major, Johnson, and arguably May who stayed largest despite losing her majority - giving something close to 50%, with the outcome depending heavily on how long the new leader waited and whether the honeymoon was banked or squandered. That 50% figure is the most defensible outside-view anchor for this question and is very close to where I have landed.

A third and increasingly relevant class is European incumbents in fragmented multi-party systems facing insurgent right challengers. Here the plurality-winner base rate is lower, nearer 35-45%, because the effective number of parties raises the variance of who finishes first. But the UK's first-past-the-post system cuts the other way: in a five-party field, plurality of seats is decided by relative efficiency of vote distribution, not by national share. That is the single most important structural fact in this question. Every seat model with post-Burnham fieldwork - Electoral Calculus 28 July, PollCheck through 29 July, Convergent Opinion MRP 25-30 July - has Labour largest by a margin of 70 to 145 seats over the next party while leading the national vote by only one to two points. Labour's 2024 coalition sits efficiently across Midlands, northern and Welsh seats; Reform's vote is broad but shallow and until recently was piling up wasted margins; the Conservative and Reform vote splitting the right across most English seats hands Labour pluralities on shares in the low twenties.

Two further empirical regularities inform the base rate. First, new-leader honeymoons decay: the historical half-life of a UK leadership bounce is roughly six to twelve months, and Burnham's is four weeks old as of today, with net ratings of +11 to +19 across Opinium, More in Common, Survation, Deltapoll and Public First. Almost none of that should be projected three years forward. Second, mid-term polling three years out is a weak predictor of election outcomes; historically the correlation between a governing party's standing at this point in the cycle and its eventual result is modest, and the typical absolute error in projecting a lead this far ahead is high single digits in vote share, which in a five-party FPTP system translates into an enormous range of seat outcomes.

Blending these: the broad incumbency class says 65-70%, the mid-term-succession class says roughly 50%, the fragmented-multi-party class says 35-45%, and the FPTP-efficiency correction pushes back up by perhaps 8-12 points from the fragmentation figure. Weighting the mid-term-succession class most heavily because it matches the actual situation, and treating the seat-efficiency advantage as the main inside-view adjustment, the outside view supports something in the high forties to low fifties. Prediction markets sit at roughly 40% normalised; Electoral Calculus's today-conditional model sits at 58%. A central estimate of 51 sits between those two anchors, closer to the midpoint than to either, which is where the evidence honestly places it.

forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
forecasts.key_change:
HOLD: 85 to 85. Nothing in the 18-19 August 2026 window moves a question whose resolution horizon is more than eight years away and whose bar is loose. The single most directly relevant observation is that the Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched successfully today at agi.goodheartlabs.com, still reads "Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 18, 2026," with an unchanged 80 percent confidence band of 2027 to 2043. That is the identical median and identical interval used in the 18 August prior. The dashboard aggregates the Metaculus weakly-general question, the Metaculus strict general-AI question, the Metaculus long adversarial Turing test question, the Manifold "AGI When? [High Quality Turing Test]" distribution, and the Kalshi "AI passes Turing test before 2030" contract, so a flat reading across the day is a genuine multi-source null rather than a stale single feed. The Metaculus strict general-AI community median remains January 2033 with roughly 25 percent by 2029 across about 1,800 to 1,900 forecasters, and the weakly-general variant remains June 2028; I could not retrieve the live Metaculus pages themselves and am relying on secondary aggregators (AIToolsReview, veracalloway, the dashboard) reporting those figures as of August 2026, so treat the precise medians as approximately rather than exactly current.

The substantive news flow in the window was safety-and-governance heavy rather than capability-declaration heavy. OpenAI published "Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities" on 18 August 2026. It confirms that the company paused reinforcement-learning training on deployment-bound models for two weeks, is holding its largest planned frontier RL run, and has left a substantial set of Astra and cyber-related workloads paused pending stronger isolation, continuous security testing and multistage monitoring. This follows the 7 August Axios exclusive that OpenAI was slowing release of Astra because internal evaluations could not rule out Critical cyber capability under its Preparedness Framework, with the blog wording implying months rather than weeks of delay. Cutting in the other direction, on 1 August OpenAI disclosed that Astra had solved ten long-open mathematics problems, including three Erdos problems, at roughly $2,000 of API cost. For the 2035 question this pair is close to a wash, and if anything mildly positive: a two-week RL pause and a months-long release delay are noise on an eight-year horizon, whereas evidence that a not-yet-released model is autonomously producing novel mathematics and plausibly crossing a Critical cyber threshold is a real capability datapoint. It does, however, establish an important structural fact - that labs are now willing to voluntarily decelerate - which matters more for near-term variants than for this one.

Anthropic's second company-wide Risk Report, published 14 August and heavily discussed on 18 August via Zvi Mowshowitz's substack write-up and secondary coverage at Unite.AI, TechTimes and Techi, raised the catastrophic-misalignment-in-high-stakes-settings rating from "very low" (February 2026) to "low". Anthropic is explicit that this reflects increased uncertainty, partly downstream of the cyber-evaluation incident disclosures, not a specific failed test or a conclusion that models became more dangerous. Two details bear on capability trajectory. First, Anthropic disclosed an unreleased internal model, "Model 2", described as somewhat more capable than frontier Mythos 5, with no current plans for external release - a second confirmation, alongside Astra, that the deployed frontier now materially lags the internal frontier. Second, and more interesting, the internal benchmark Anthropic built to detect whether its most dangerous capability threshold has been crossed has saturated and can no longer register incremental gains, at the same time as the company reports early signs of acceleration. Benchmark saturation at the safety-critical end is a modest positive for capability timelines and a clear negative for measurability, which is one reason I do not treat it as worth more than a fraction of a point.

On capability benchmarks generally, the picture in August 2026 is bifurcated and unchanged in the window. ARC-AGI-2 is effectively falling: as of 7 August GPT-5.6 Sol leads at 92.5 percent, Claude Opus 5 at 90.4 percent and GPT-5.5 at 85 percent, against average individual human performance of 66 percent and an 85 percent grand-prize threshold. ARC-AGI-3, by contrast, still has frontier systems scoring under 1 percent. Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash on 13 August with FrontierCode 1.1 Main at 43.6 percent (up from 34.4 percent for 3.6 Flash three weeks earlier), Terminal-bench 2.1 at 85.8 percent, DeepSWE v1.1 at 65.3 percent and AutomationBench at 30.4 percent. Rapid gains on coding and agentic benchmarks alongside near-zero performance on novel fluid-reasoning tasks is exactly the pattern that keeps the strict-definition distributions wide and is the main reason my central estimate is not higher.

The one arguably negative dated item is compute. Fortune reported on 18 August 2026 that the OpenAI-Nvidia Ohio arrangement "comes in $145 billion lower than reported", framing it as a signal of concerns about artificial demand for chips. The confirmed structure, per the 17 August securities filing covered by CNBC, Bloomberg, Axios and UPI, is a backstop of up to $105 billion of OpenAI lease and power obligations to SB Energy at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County over a 20-year lease, supporting an initial 4.25 GW with an option for a further 3.75 GW, phased online from 2028, plus a $1.5 billion Nvidia equity investment in SB Energy. Nvidia had previously discussed a backstop of up to $250 billion for a 10 GW buildout, and reports on 10 August already indicated a cut below $120 billion. So the news is that a very large buildout got somewhat smaller, not that it was cancelled: 4.25 GW firm with an option to roughly double is still one of the largest single compute commitments ever, and it is a guarantee rather than cash, which is precisely why the headline number is elastic. Against a 2035 horizon, a step-down from a speculative $250 billion figure to a contracted $105 billion is worth well under a point.

I also checked for the two things that would actually move this question - a lab announcing AGI, or three or more leading researchers stating AGI has been achieved - and found nothing new on 18 or 19 August. The standing precedent remains Jensen Huang's March 2026 "we've achieved AGI" remark, which Fortune covered on 30 March 2026 alongside the observation that nobody agrees what the term means, and which was publicly contested by researchers proposing new measurement schemes. That episode is informative for the resolution criteria: the announcement bar here is genuinely low, and definitional drift is a live pathway to YES independent of any strict capability threshold. On the timeline-revision side, the most recent systematic tracker I could fetch is FutureSearch's, last modified 12 April 2026, which reports that every forecaster who updated between January and April 2026 moved sooner, after a 2025 period in which Kokotajlo, Lifland, Amodei, Wildeford and the Metaculus community all moved later. No update to that tracker appeared in the window. Sources I could not fetch directly: Metaculus question pages, Kalshi and Polymarket order books, and llm-stats.com (bot check). Kalshi's OpenAI-AGI-by-2030 contract is reported at roughly 55 percent and Polymarket's OpenAI-AGI-by-2027 at roughly 9 to 11 percent, both from secondary summaries rather than live quotes.
forecasts.base_rate:
The question does not have a clean historical reference class - AGI has never been developed, so frequency-based base rates are unavailable. The usable outside view is therefore the distribution of published forecasts on near-identical questions, treated as a reference class of forecaster distributions rather than of events.

The primary anchor is the Goodheart Labs combined dashboard, which as of 18 August 2026 gives a median arrival year of 2031 with an 80 percent interval of 2027 to 2043. Fitting a right-skewed distribution to those three points - 10th percentile 2027, 50th percentile 2031, 90th percentile 2043 - places roughly 68 to 75 percent of the mass before 1 January 2035. The distribution is highly asymmetric: only four years separate the 10th and 50th percentiles but twelve separate the 50th and 90th, so the cumulative mass climbs steeply through the early 2030s and then flattens.

The second anchor is Metaculus's strict "first general AI system devised, tested and publicly announced" question, with a community median of January 2033 across roughly 1,800 to 1,900 forecasters and about 25 percent by 2029. A median of early 2033 mechanically implies more than 50 percent by 2035; interpolating the shape of that community distribution suggests something in the 60 to 70 percent range by 1 January 2035. This is the most conservative credible anchor because Metaculus's four-condition operationalisation - including a long adversarial Turing test, robotic manipulation, and unified model performance across several hard benchmarks - is far stricter than this question's resolution criteria. The Metaculus weakly-general variant, median June 2028, sits at the other end and implies well over 90 percent by 2035.

The third anchor is market pricing. Manifold's high-quality-Turing-test AGI distribution puts roughly 50 percent on before 2030. Kalshi's OpenAI-AGI-by-2030 contract has traded in the 44 to 55 percent range through 2026, most recently reported near 55 percent. Polymarket's OpenAI-AGI-by-2027 market sits near 9 to 11 percent. Markets that price roughly half the probability mass inside the next four years leave very little room for the residual to survive a further five, unless one believes in a hard structural ceiling.

The fourth anchor is expert timelines: frontier-lab leadership clusters at 2026 to 2028, aggregated community forecasts around 2031 to 2033, and named sceptics at 2035 or later. FutureSearch's tracker, using the definition "most purely cognitive labor is automatable at better quality, speed and cost than humans", shows the 2023-2025 direction of travel was strongly toward sooner, a 2025 reversal outward for Kokotajlo, Lifland, Amodei, Wildeford and the Metaculus community, and then a renewed inward move by everyone who updated between January and April 2026.

The critical adjustment is definitional. This question resolves on a credible lab publicly announcing AGI, or three or more leading researchers publicly stating AGI has been achieved. That is a social and rhetorical threshold, not a capability threshold, and it is strictly easier to clear than any of the operationalised benchmarks above. Jensen Huang already said in March 2026 that AGI has been achieved; Dario Amodei has publicly described a "nation of geniuses in a data centre" as likely by 2027. Labs have strong commercial and narrative incentives to claim the milestone, and the term has no agreed definition to police the claim against. I therefore add roughly 12 to 18 percentage points to the capability-satisfaction base rate of about 70 percent, arriving at a central estimate in the mid-80s. The main brake on going higher is the possibility that the field deliberately abandons or fractures the term, so that no lab makes a clean announcement and no coherent set of three researchers converges on the statement - which is a real risk given the current preference for graded taxonomies over a single threshold.

forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
HOLD: 7 to 7. The 18-19 August 2026 window produced a moderate volume of dated, checkable material, but nothing that changes the structural picture of a coercion campaign that remains intense, expanding in the maritime-legal domain, and still entirely below the threshold this question asks about. Taking the items in order. Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense reported, in its post to X on 19 August 2026, 20 sorties of PLA aircraft, 7 PLAN vessels and 6 official (coast guard/maritime) ships around Taiwan up to 0600 UTC+8, with 15 of the 20 sorties entering the northern, central, southwestern and eastern ADIZ. That is a four-fold jump on the 18 August figure carried in the prior forecast (5 sorties, 8 PLAN vessels, 7 official ships, 3 sorties into northern/eastern ADIZ) and a twenty-fold jump on 17 August (1 sortie, 9 PLAN vessels, 7 official ships). Read against the wider mid-August series, the 19 August number is unremarkable: MND logged 11 aircraft and 8 PLAN vessels on 16 August with 7 median-line crossings, 4 aircraft and 8 vessels on 15 August, and 9 aircraft and 12 vessels on 14 August. The August 2026 range is roughly 1 to 20 sorties per day against a 2024-25 baseline that frequently exceeded 20-30 and spiked above 40. A single 20-sortie day is inside the noise band and I have deliberately not updated on it. Notably, the 19 August MND text does not describe a median-line crossing count separately, only ADIZ entries, so I cannot confirm from the ANI relay whether crossings rose in proportion.

The most substantive analytical input in the window is the joint AEI-Institute for the Study of War China & Taiwan Update dated 18 August 2026 (data cutoff 17 August), which I fetched in full. Its three toplines are the Legislative Yuan's passage on 14 August of the NT$2.99 trillion (US$93bn) 2026 general budget after a record 350-day delay, including the full NT$44.2bn (US$1.38bn) drone-industry budget and NT$19.2bn (US$600m) in procurement, with a 2.5 percent cut to military equipment and facilities; Philippine President Marcos's 14 August statement that "there will be no attacks on anyone from the Philippines" during a PRC invasion of Taiwan, alongside a sought "reset" with Beijing and possible joint South China Sea oil and gas exploration; and an assessment that the PRC will use Taiwan's 2026 local elections, especially the Kaohsiung mayoral race, as a testing ground for interference operations, citing Liberty Times reporting of 10 August that the CCP's Beidaihe retreat (begun 3 August) set electing "patriotic forces" in Taiwan in 2026 as a near-term objective. Crucially, the ISW-AEI update contains no invasion or blockade warning indicators: no mobilisation, no reserve call-up, no shipping or NOTAM closures, no announced named exercise. Its other items are a suspected PRC AI-agent cyberattack that mapped 21 Taiwanese government systems in early July, compromised 85 accounts and extracted 2,500 personnel records; a Vatn Systems-NCSIST memorandum of 11 August on S12 autonomous UUVs; a US-Taiwan coast guard training course running 10-21 August; and PRC seabed "lawnmower" surveying near Palau and Guam.

Three further dated items matter more for the tails. First, and most consequential: between 15 and 16 August 2026 the United States began redeploying USS George Washington, its last carrier in Asia, from Japan through the Singapore Strait (entered 13 August) to the Middle East to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln in the Iran campaign, leaving the western Pacific without a US carrier. Axios covered this on 17 August; TWZ's carrier tracker of 17 August and Forbes on 13 August corroborate. Global Times ran a triumphalist piece framing it as "the bill for overstretch." This is a genuine, if temporary, window-of-opportunity signal and the strongest upward item in the window. I weight it modestly: carrier gaps in Asia also occurred in 2024 without incident, a Taiwan campaign requires months of observable preparation that has not begun, and the gap is expected to be measured in weeks. Second, the Iran war itself (Strait of Hormuz closure prompted a Philippine energy emergency on 24 March 2026) is absorbing US naval capacity and is the main structural reason for the gap. Third, on the de-escalatory side, the White House and Secretary of State Rubio have confirmed Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States on 24 September 2026, the third Trump-Xi meeting of the term, following the May 2026 Beijing summit at which Xi called Taiwan "the most important issue" and warned of collision. Nations do not typically initiate blockades five weeks before a state visit they are actively preparing.

On the coercion-infrastructure side, the trend continues to build without crossing thresholds. Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration announced new Taiwan Strait traffic-control measures on 14 August, nominally typhoon-related but read by analysts as a jurisdiction test. PRC state media on 14 August framed a 12 August PRC-Indonesian naval passing exercise east of Taiwan as demonstrating PRC jurisdiction over Taiwan's eastern EEZ; Jakarta publicly downplayed it on 16 August as a routine goodwill engagement in international waters, which is a meaningful rebuff. China Coast Guard has run regular patrols east of Taiwan since June-July 2026, condemned by Rubio. Taiwan ran an anti-blockade merchant-escort drill on 13 August during Han Kuang, which concluded 14 August. Set against this, SCMP reporting notes PLA fighter sorties near Taiwan fell to a three-year low in H1 2026 and that the PLA staged no large-scale named drills around the island in that period, the first such stretch since 2022 — a materially dovish operational-tempo datapoint that offsets the maritime-legal escalation.

Market and forecast-community evidence: Polymarket's "invade Taiwan by 30 September 2026" market sat at roughly 98.8 percent No on about US$1.86m volume as of 12 August 2026, and end-2026 at roughly 96 percent No. I could not directly fetch Metaculus or Polymarket pages (the Metaculus API URL was outside the fetch provenance set), so these figures come from search summaries and secondary crypto-press aggregation and should be treated as indicative only. Search-surfaced Metaculus figures for 2030-horizon invasion questions ranged from 22 to 43 percent, but those questions are differently worded (some include any armed conflict or partial control) and I do not treat them as comparable to this resolution criterion. Sources I could fetch directly and rely on: AEI/ISW 18 August, ANI relay of MND 19 August, SecurityStudies.info Asia-Pacific briefing of 16 August, GlobalSecurity/Global Times of 11 August, armedconflicts.org tracker refreshed 19 August. Sources I could not fetch: Metaculus, Polymarket, Reuters and Taipei Times originals, PRC MND and Taiwan Affairs Office primary transcripts. Net: one modest upward item (carrier gap), one modest downward item (September summit on track, low PLA sortie tempo), and a large volume of confirmatory gray-zone noise. Hold at 7.
forecasts.base_rate:
Two reference classes anchor this forecast, and they agree on a low-single-digit answer.

The broad class is major-power initiation of an opposed amphibious assault, or a sustained naval blockade of a defended, populated territory, since 1945. Candidate cases are few: Inchon 1950 (against a state at war), Suez 1956, the Cuban missile "quarantine" of 1962 (a partial interdiction lasting under a month), Falklands 1982 (a British counter-invasion of a small garrisoned archipelago), the Iran-Iraq tanker war of 1984-88, and Russia's Black Sea grain interdiction from 2022. Over roughly 80 years and a small number of dyads with both the capability and the claimed casus belli, the annualised hazard for any given capable-power/target pair is on the order of 0.5 to 2 percent. Applied to the 3.4 years from 19 August 2026 to 1 January 2030, that yields roughly 2 to 7 percent. Blockade is the more common and more available option than assault, which is why a question that resolves on either is somewhat higher than an invasion-only question. Amphibious assault against a defended island of 23 million people with 130km of open water, adverse weather windows and a mountainous eastern coast is a categorically harder operation than anything attempted since 1945, and no state has attempted one at this scale.

The narrow, better-matched class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes since 1995. The list: the 1995 and 1996 missile crises; the August 2022 Pelosi-visit encirclement exercises; Joint Sword 2024A in May 2024 and Joint Sword 2024B in October 2024; Strait Thunder 2025A in April 2025; and Justice Mission 2025. Seven salient episodes across roughly 31 years. Every one was time-boxed (hours to days), announced or acknowledged as an exercise, and reversible; none involved boarding, interdiction of commercial shipping, or a declared closure lasting beyond 72 hours; none escalated to assault. Zero for seven. A Laplace-style estimate of the per-episode conditional probability that a coercion episode converts into a >72-hour blockade or an assault gives roughly 1/(7+2) = 11 percent per episode; at an observed rate of roughly 0.5 to 1 salient episodes per year over the recent period, and with the 2026 tempo running below trend (no large-scale named drill in H1 2026, the first such gap since 2022; PLA fighter sorties at a three-year low), the expected number of conversion opportunities in the remaining 3.4 years is perhaps 2 to 4, giving 4 to 9 percent. That range brackets the central estimate.

Three adjustments to the base rate. Upward: the PLA is on a publicly reported trajectory toward "being capable" of a Taiwan operation by 2027, per successive US Department of Defense assessments; capability growth mechanically raises the ceiling even if intent is unchanged. The PRC is also building non-kinetic quarantine infrastructure — China Coast Guard patrols east of Taiwan since June-July 2026, Guangdong MSA traffic-control announcements, "law enforcement" framing, scientific survey missions — which lowers the operational and political cost of a quarantine that could satisfy this question's blockade limb if sustained past 72 hours. Downward: the resolution bar is high and specific. A quarantine that Beijing frames as customs inspection, or an exercise-style encirclement of 48-72 hours, both of which are more likely than a true blockade, would probably not resolve YES; two major agencies would have to characterise it as a blockade exceeding 72 hours or an assault on Taiwan proper. Also downward: PRC economic dependence on semiconductors, exposure to sanctions, an unresolved property and demographic drag, and a demonstrated preference through 2026 for political-warfare tools — election interference around the November 2026 local elections, AI-enabled cyber operations, legal and maritime accretion — over kinetic action.

Structural uncertainty: the reference class is thin, the outcome is heavily dependent on the private intentions of one decision-maker, and historical base rates poorly capture regime-level discontinuities. Published superforecaster and expert-elicitation work on Taiwan through 2030 clusters roughly in the 5 to 20 percent band for invasion-or-blockade questions, with prediction markets consistently at the low end (Polymarket implying about 4 percent for a 2026 invasion as of mid-August 2026). I sit slightly below the middle of that expert band because of the strictness of the >72-hour and "assault on Taiwan proper" criteria, and because the 0-for-7 Strait record is the single most informative piece of evidence available.

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: HOLD: 1 to 1, with the 80% interval narrowed from [0, 2] to [0, 1]. The July 2026 print published on schedule at 7:00am today, 19 August 2026, and it did not surprise to the downside. It surprised, mildly, to the upside of the Bank of England's own path and squarely in line with the economist consensus: UK CPI rose 2.9% in the 12 months to July 2026, up from 2.6% in June, the highest annual rate since March 2026 and 0.9 percentage points above the level this question requires. Consensus going into the print was 2.9% (Pantheon Macroeconomics and Deutsche Bank both published 2.9%), so the headline came in as expected, but the Bank of England's own July Monetary Policy Report profile had implied around 2.8%, meaning the outturn was a touch hotter than the official forecast. Core CPI held at 2.6% year on year, against a consensus of 2.5% and a Deutsche Bank call of 2.5%, so the underlying picture was firmer than expected too. Core CPIH rose to 2.9% from 2.8%. The composition is exactly what was anticipated in yesterday's reasoning: the largest upward contribution came from housing and household services, whose annual rate jumped to 4.1% from 2.7% in June, driven by gas prices up 14.7% and electricity up 3.6%. That reflects Ofgem's energy price cap rising 13% on 1 July, which lifted the typical dual-fuel direct-debit bill by GBP 221 to GBP 1,862. The one genuinely disinflationary element was services: the CPI services annual rate eased to 3.4% from 3.6%, matching Pantheon's call, and that easing was driven largely by an air-fares base effect, with fares up 11.7% between June and July 2026 against 30.2% in the same window of 2025. Robert Wood at Pantheon explicitly flagged that the services softening reflects temporary factors that will unwind over the summer, so it is not evidence of a durable disinflationary turn. The arithmetic of what remains is now considerably worse for YES than it was yesterday. With the July print banked, only four reference months can still publish before 1 January 2027: August (due mid-September), September (due 21 October 2026), October (due 18 November 2026) and November (due mid-December 2026). December 2026 publishes in January 2027 and is out of scope. Working in index terms using the ONS series, CPI stood at 138.9 in June 2025, 139.0 in July 2025, 139.3 in August and September 2025, 139.8 in October 2025 and 139.5 in November 2025; June 2026 was 142.5, and a 2.9% annual rate in July 2026 implies an index of roughly 143.0. To print an annual rate that rounds below 2.0%, the index would need to fall below about 142.0 in August or September, below about 142.5 in October, and below about 142.2 in November. From 143.0 that means the price level would have to fall by roughly 0.7% over one to two months, or by roughly 0.3% to 0.6% cumulatively over three to four months, at a time of year when the index normally rises. Nothing in the forward calendar points that way. Cornwall Insight's latest October cap forecast, published after the government's VAT announcement, is GBP 1,699.59 for October to December 2026, revised down from GBP 1,906.27, but the revision reflects the removal of 5% VAT on domestic electricity plus Ofgem's rebasing of typical household consumption, and Cornwall still expects the October cap to sit about 2% above the current level on a like-for-like basis because of Middle East-driven wholesale gas strength. Ofgem confirms the October cap by 26 August 2026. The VAT measure itself, announced on 21 July 2026 as one of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first acts and effective 1 October 2026, is the single largest genuinely disinflationary event in the window, and the government's own costing puts its effect at roughly 0.10 percentage points off CPI, worth about GBP 45 off the annual cap. That is one-ninth of the gap that would need to close. Official and market forecasts point the other way entirely. The Bank's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report, published 30 July, has CPI peaking at around 3.2% in 2026 Q4, with the MPC noting risks to that projection tilted to the upside. HM Treasury's panel of independent forecasters averaged 3.7% for Q4 2026 in the 17 June survey and around 3.5% in the May survey. Deutsche Bank sees a 3.3% to 3.5% peak in Q4. In other words, the modal published path for every one of the four remaining reference months is materially above July's 2.9%, not below 2.0%. The policy signal is consistent: the MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% for a fifth consecutive meeting on 30 July on a 6-3 vote, more divided than the 7-2 expected, and Governor Bailey said explicitly that if the Middle East conflict persists and second-round effects emerge the Bank will likely need to raise rates. Market commentary today frames the September 17 meeting as a live hike risk, not a cut. A central bank contemplating tightening is not a central bank that expects sub-2% prints within four months. Genuine offsets exist but are small relative to the gap. Grocery inflation, per Worldpanel by Numerator, slowed to 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August 2026 from 2.6% in the four weeks to 12 July, the lowest since October 2024 and a fifth consecutive monthly deceleration; food carries roughly an 11% CPI weight, so even a full percentage point of further food disinflation is worth around 0.1pp. The goods annual rate had slowed to 1.7% in June. Labour market data released ahead of today's print was described as soft, which over time compresses services inflation. But these are 2027 stories on the published paths, not 2026 ones. Set against them, oil rose about 22% on the renewed Middle East hostilities, Brent was around USD 87 as of mid-August, and President Trump has ruled out extending the Iran ceasefire, keeping the energy impulse live into the autumn assessment window that determines the January 2027 cap. The net effect of today is not to change the direction of the forecast but to remove the last plausible route to YES. Yesterday the question was whether five prints starting from 2.6% could deliver 0.65pp of disinflation. Today it is whether four prints starting from 2.9% can deliver 0.95pp, with the October cap rising, oil elevated, the BoE forecasting a Q4 peak above 3%, and consensus above that. My unrounded point estimate has moved from roughly 0.8% to roughly 0.3%. That still rounds to 1 at integer resolution, and I am holding at 1 rather than dropping to 0 because four unobserved prints remain and a zero would assert impossibility: a sudden Middle East de-escalation collapsing gas, a large emergency energy or VAT package at the Autumn Budget, or an ONS reweighting or data incident are each individually improbable but not excluded. The substantive update is in the interval, which I am cutting to [0, 1]: a 2% upper bound is no longer defensible now that the starting point is 2.9% and the official central path is 3.2%.
forecasts.base_rate: The natural reference class is the historical frequency with which UK CPI annual inflation has fallen below 2.0% within a four-month horizon starting from a reading of 2.9% or higher. Using the ONS CPI series from 1989 onwards, months in which the annual rate stood between 2.7% and 3.1% number in the low hundreds; the share of those in which the annual rate printed below 2.0% at any point in the following four months is on the order of 5-8%. That is the raw outside view and it is already low. It is also almost certainly an overstatement here, for three reasons. First, the historical episodes that delivered such rapid disinflation were overwhelmingly driven by sharp downside energy shocks or demand collapses: late 2008 into 2009, when CPI fell from 3.1% in September 2009-adjacent readings amid the financial crisis and a VAT cut; mid-2013 to 2015, when the oil price halved; and 2020, when the pandemic and the Eat Out to Help Out and VAT measures compressed the index. None of these conditions is present. The current shock is a positive energy shock, not a negative one, with oil up roughly 22% on the Middle East conflict and Ofgem's July cap up 13%. Second, the administered-price calendar inside the window points up rather than down. The October price cap, confirmed by Ofgem by 26 August 2026, is forecast by Cornwall Insight to rise about 2% on a like-for-like basis even after the electricity VAT cut, so the single largest scheduled price event in the window is inflationary on net. Third, a much tighter reference class is available and it is more informative than the historical frequency: the distribution of published forecasts for the specific months in question. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report central projection has CPI peaking around 3.2% in 2026 Q4; HM Treasury's June panel of independent forecasters averaged 3.7% for Q4 2026 and around 3.5% in May; Deutsche Bank projects a 3.3-3.5% Q4 peak. Not one publicly identifiable institutional forecast has any month between August and November 2026 below 2.0%. Historically, the standard deviation of one-quarter-ahead CPI forecast errors for the UK is roughly 0.3-0.4pp, larger in energy-shock periods. Treating the BoE's roughly 3.1-3.2% central path for the relevant months and asking for the probability of any single month landing below 1.95% requires an error of about 1.2pp, or three to four standard deviations, in the disinflationary direction. Even allowing for four correlated attempts and fat tails, that maps to well under 1%. A third, cruder reference class is the base rate at which a monthly CPI index falls outright over a summer-to-autumn stretch. UK CPI index falls of 0.3% or more between July and November have essentially not occurred outside 2008-09 and 2020 in the post-1997 inflation-targeting era; the seasonal pattern is mildly positive over that span. Combining these, the outside view sits at roughly 0.5-2% before inside-view adjustment, and the inside-view adjustments (energy cap rising in October, oil elevated, services at 3.4% and described as temporarily soft, core sticky at 2.6%, a central bank debating a hike) all cut in the same direction. The reference-class limitation worth flagging is that policy interventions are poorly captured: the UK has twice in twenty years used VAT to move CPI sharply (December 2008 and July 2020), and a new administration under Prime Minister Burnham has already cut electricity VAT once, with an Autumn Budget still to come. That is the main channel keeping the estimate above zero rather than at zero, but the electricity VAT cut itself is worth only about 0.10pp on the government's own costing, so an intervention nine times larger would be needed.

forecasts.question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
HOLD at 100. Both resolution sources were reachable today and both report the identical cumulative worldwide figure, which sits roughly 35 percent above the $1.5B threshold. The Numbers (https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/spider-man-brand-new-day-(2026)), retrieved 19 August 2026, reports Domestic $794,051,866, International $1,236,000,000 and Worldwide $2,030,051,866, with the tracked report date on the domestic daily table advancing to 8/18/2026. Box Office Mojo (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt22084616/), retrieved 19 August 2026, reports the same three numbers to the dollar: Domestic $794,051,866, International $1,236,000,000, Worldwide $2,030,051,866. Note that Box Office Mojo's summary figures did not render through the plain page-extraction path (the aggregate table returned em-dashes, and the release-level page rl2299756545 returned "There is no data to display"), so the figures above were pulled from the raw title-page HTML via a direct request with a browser user-agent. That is a rendering artefact of the extraction method, not a data outage; the underlying page carries the numbers. I flag it because a naive retrieval on a future day could produce a spurious "source unreachable" or "source blank" reading, and the correct interpretation in that event is instrument failure rather than a restatement.

The delta since the 18 August snapshot is +$7,219,866 worldwide, from $2,022,832,000 to $2,030,051,866. Every dollar of that movement is domestic: the domestic line moved from $786,832,000 to $794,051,866, exactly +$7,219,866, while the international line is unchanged at $1,236,000,000. That pattern is the expected one. The Numbers refreshes domestic daily and international on a weekly-ish cadence tied to studio international reporting, so a flat international line on a Wednesday carries no information about foreign performance; it simply means the overseas cume has not been restated since the last international update. The domestic increment is consistent with a film in its third full week posting mid-week grosses in the $7M range against a $794M cume, which is a normal decay profile and irrelevant to resolution either way. It is also worth noting that the prior day's figures as recorded were round to the nearest thousand on domestic and worldwide, whereas today's are dollar-exact on both sources; the small apparent tidiness of yesterday's numbers reflects how they were transcribed, not a change in source precision.

The residual risk analysis is unchanged in structure and, if anything, marginally tighter than yesterday. Resolution requires the published worldwide cumulative on Box Office Mojo or The Numbers to exceed $1.5B at some point on or before 31 December 2026. That condition is already satisfied and has been continuously satisfied since roughly 13-14 August, when the film crossed $2B. The question does not require the figure to still be above $1.5B on 31 December; it requires the gross to have exceeded $1.5B by that date, and a cumulative gross is monotonically non-decreasing in normal accounting. So the only paths to NO are (a) a catastrophic downward restatement of about 26 percent of the published worldwide total, sustained through year end and reflected on both sources, or (b) a resolution-mechanics failure in which neither source is consultable or a resolver reads the question in some perverse way. Neither is a live concern. On (a), major-studio worldwide cumes are compiled from Comscore domestic actuals and studio-reported international actuals; downward revisions do occur, but they are of the order of hundreds of thousands to low single-digit millions, typically when an estimate is trued up to actuals or a territory is reclassified. A $530M haircut has no precedent for any wide release, let alone one whose milestones have been independently confirmed by Variety, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter trade reporting. The redundancy in the resolution clause helps further: the question resolves YES on either source, so a data error confined to one aggregator cannot flip it. Today both sources agree to the dollar, which is itself weak evidence that the underlying feed is clean rather than one site carrying a stale or mis-keyed figure.

On (b), the extraction friction on Box Office Mojo noted above is the only observable that moved at all today, and it points at my retrieval method rather than at the source. The Numbers resolved cleanly on the first attempt. Even in a scenario where Box Office Mojo went dark permanently, The Numbers alone satisfies the resolution criterion, and vice versa. Trade press has independently and repeatedly recorded the $1B international and $2B worldwide milestones, so the factual record would survive the loss of both aggregators for any reasonable adjudication.

The forecast therefore stays at 100 with an 80% CI of [100, 100]. As stated yesterday, 100 here is a rounding of a probability above 99.9%, not a claim of logical certainty. The skill's guidance against extreme probabilities without extreme evidence is satisfied: the evidence is that the outcome has already occurred and is published on both named resolution sources with a 35 percent margin over the threshold, cross-confirmed by three independent trade outlets. Holding anything meaningfully below 100 would be a failure of calibration in the other direction, paying a scoring penalty for a hedge against an event with no reference-class instances. The only remaining function of continued daily monitoring is to catch a resolution-mechanics anomaly, not to track box office performance, which has been irrelevant to this question for about a week.
forecasts.base_rate:
The naive reference class for this question is "wide-release tentpole films that reach $1.5B worldwide," which historically is a small set: fewer than fifteen titles in cinema history have crossed $1.5B, and the unconditional base rate for any given tentpole is low single digits. That class is the correct one to reason from before release, and it would have been the right frame for this question in, say, June 2026. It is the wrong class now, and using it would be a textbook base-rate error of the type superforecasters guard against: applying a reference class that ignores the most informative available conditioning information.

The governing reference class today is "published box office milestones on a major aggregator that are subsequently restated below the milestone threshold." The event has already happened. Spider-Man: Brand New Day crossed $1.5B worldwide in roughly its second week of release and is now at $2.03B on both named sources. The question is no longer forecasting a future gross; it is forecasting whether an already-published, independently corroborated cumulative figure gets revised downward by about 26 percent and stays revised through 31 December 2026, on both Box Office Mojo and The Numbers simultaneously.

I know of no instance of this. Box office aggregators do revise figures. The typical mechanism is that Sunday weekend estimates issued by studios are replaced with Monday actuals, which historically move by roughly plus or minus one to three percent, and occasionally more for a film with an unusual holiday or preview pattern. Longer-run revisions occur when international territories are trued up, when a re-release is folded in or split out, or when a distributor reclassifies which markets count as domestic. The magnitudes are almost always under one percent of cume for a film past its opening month. Documented larger disputes exist in the historical record, mostly involving contested inflation-adjusted rankings, Chinese reporting for certain local titles, or older films where the studio's own historical accounting was unclear. None of those involve a live 2026 Hollywood tentpole with Comscore-sourced domestic actuals, and none produced a 26 percent downward restatement.

A second useful class is "questions whose resolution condition is already met at the time of forecast, with an open window remaining." For genuinely monotone quantities like cumulative gross, cumulative cases, or cumulative funds raised, the historical resolution rate of such questions is effectively one hundred percent, with the rare exceptions arising from ambiguity in the question wording or from a resolver applying a different source than the one anticipated. Here the wording is clean, the threshold is a simple dollar figure, and the sources are named explicitly with an "or" between them, which supplies redundancy. There is no measurement window subtlety: the phrase "by 31 December 2026" is a deadline for the event, not a snapshot test on that date.

A third relevant class is "aggregator availability." Both Box Office Mojo, owned by IMDb and Amazon, and The Numbers, run by Nash Information Services, have been continuously operating for decades. Extended simultaneous unavailability through year end is a sub-0.1 percent proposition, and even that would not obviously produce a NO given the corroborating trade reporting from Variety, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter, all of which published the $2B milestone in August 2026.

Combining: the conditional base rate for a NO, given an already-published cumulative 35 percent above threshold on two independent sources, is bounded above by the historical frequency of catastrophic aggregator restatements, which is zero over a large denominator of milestone crossings. Applying a Laplace-style correction over a conservative denominator of, say, several hundred milestone crossings across the modern era gives an upper bound of a few tenths of a percent, and that estimate is itself dominated by generic model-uncertainty rather than by any specific pathway. The resulting forecast is above 99.9 percent, which rounds to 100 on an integer scale.
