forecasts.question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
HOLD: 99 to 99. Nothing in the 18-19 August window moves the combined run-rate arithmetic below the $70bn bar; the day's biggest story was about the split between the two companies, not the total. Dated items follow. First, the Wall Street Journal, 18 August 2026, "OpenAI's Second-Quarter Sales Show Tepid Growth Compared With Anthropic": OpenAI generated $6.7bn of revenue in the three months to June, up from $5.7bn in Q1, an 18% sequential increase, while its operating loss including stock-based compensation widened to $12.3bn from $9.3bn. The same report puts Anthropic's Q2 revenue at $11.6bn with an operating profit of $559m, the first quarter in which Anthropic's sales exceeded OpenAI's. I could not fetch the WSJ piece directly (hard paywall); I verified the figures through SiliconANGLE's full-text write-up (Mike Wheatley, published 19 August 01:25 UTC, which links and quotes the WSJ story), plus Investing.com, PYMNTS and a KuCoin newswire flash, all consistent on $6.7bn, $5.7bn, 18%, $12.3bn, $9.3bn, $11.6bn and $559m. Second, SiliconANGLE adds that OpenAI told investors privately its growth rate has accelerated since the July model generation launched, without supplying numbers, and notes chief revenue officer Denise Dresser's departure after less than a year, following Brad Lightcap and Fidji Simo. Third, Forbes (Jon Markman, 18 August) and Fortune (18 August) both published follow-ups on Anthropic's $65bn run rate; neither carries a new figure. Fourth, Bloomberg Television ran "Anthropic's $65 Billion Surge, OpenAI's Teen Push" on 18 August, again a restatement. Fifth, I fetched the Axios piece (Madison Mills, 17 August, free) in full: it confirms Anthropic's preliminary Q2 revenue above $11.5bn per documents seen by Bloomberg, Q1 of $4.73bn implying a sequential increase above 140%, the $65bn run rate reached at end-July, and OpenAI's $40bn run rate per Greg Brockman's internal message. Axios explicitly flags that the two companies may not measure revenue the same way, and reports Anthropic meeting new investors ahead of an IPO expected September or October with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, and OpenAI on track to draw over half its revenue from enterprise by year end. Sixth, no public S-1 exists for either company as of 19 August; Anthropic's confidential draft was submitted 1 June 2026 and OpenAI's in early June, with reporting since late June that OpenAI may push its listing to 2027 rather than accept below a $1trn valuation. Seventh, the other OpenAI items dated 18 August are non-financial: the guardrailed junior version of ChatGPT launched, some training runs were paused over cybersecurity concerns, and on 17 August it leased a 10GW data centre campus from SoftBank's SB Energy.

The arithmetic is unchanged. On exit run rate, the measure the resolution language points at when it says ARR, Anthropic is above $65bn as of end-July (Bloomberg, 17 August) and OpenAI is above $40bn as of mid-August (Bloomberg, 13 August, sourced to Brockman's internal note that monthly run rate grew more than 20% in July alone). Combined, roughly $105bn against a $70bn threshold, a cushion of $35bn. For NO, the pair would have to shed a third of their combined run rate in the four and a half months to 31 December while both are mid-IPO-process and both are still growing. That is not a forecastable event; it is a discontinuity.

The one genuinely new consideration from 18 August is the gap between recognised revenue and claimed run rate at OpenAI. Four times Q2 revenue is $26.8bn, well short of the $40bn run rate, which tells you the $40bn is an exit-month annualisation rather than a trailing figure. Anthropic shows the same pattern less severely: four times $11.6bn is $46.4bn against a $65bn end-July run rate. If a resolver perversely used trailing-quarter-annualised revenue instead of ARR, the Q2 combined figure would be $18.3bn times four, or $73.2bn, still above $70bn but with only about 4.5% headroom. That is worth naming, but it cuts the right way over the remaining horizon: the question resolves on Q4, not Q2. For a Q4-actual-annualised reading to fail, combined Q4 revenue would have to come in below $17.5bn, against $18.3bn already booked in Q2 and with Anthropic having grown 140% sequentially into that quarter. Anthropic alone at roughly $16-18bn in Q3 would annualise to $64-72bn. So both the run-rate reading and the recognised-revenue reading point YES, the first with an enormous margin and the second with a comfortable and widening one.

Downside items I actively looked for and found: Ed Zitron's "Anthropic's Profitability Swindle" and institutional commentary on gross-versus-net treatment, front-loaded annual commitments, and the timing of the SpaceX compute contract, all arguing Anthropic's reported revenue and its Q2 operating profit flatter the underlying business; the WSJ's evidence that ChatGPT growth has stalled and that OpenAI cut prices on two recent models as enterprises shifted workloads to cheaper open-source and Chinese systems; and OpenAI's IPO slippage. None of these plausibly removes a third of the combined figure. Stress test the worst credible version: if a public S-1 forced Anthropic onto a strict net basis and halved its reported number to $32.5bn, adding OpenAI's $40bn still yields $72.5bn and the question still resolves YES. Halving both is the only path to NO, and no source suggests anything of the kind. Residual probability mass sits with resolver ambiguity, a restatement of both companies simultaneously, and genuine catastrophic tails, which together I keep at roughly 1%. Holding at 99 with the interval at 98 to 99.
forecasts.base_rate:
The governing reference class is not "will two companies grow to a threshold" but "a threshold has already been crossed on the published record with substantial headroom; will it still be crossed at the measurement date". This is a persistence question, and persistence questions of this shape resolve YES at very high rates. Across forecasting platforms, questions where the resolution condition is already satisfied by roughly 50% margin four to five months before the deadline, in a domain with monotonic underlying trend and no mechanism for reversal, resolve YES in the high nineties. The correct anchor is 97-99%, and the residual is dominated by resolution-mechanics failure rather than by the world changing.

Three narrower classes support the same reading. First, revenue trajectories of large private technology companies at $10bn-plus scale. Instances of a firm's disclosed annualised revenue falling by more than 30% within two quarters, absent fraud or an exogenous demand collapse, are close to unrepresented. The cases that exist are Wirecard and FTX, where the revenue was substantially fictitious, and the 2020 travel and hospitality shock, where the demand base physically disappeared. Neither template maps onto enterprise AI subscriptions and API consumption in the back half of 2026, where the observable direction of travel is enterprise budget expansion and multi-year commitments. Base rate of a 33% two-quarter contraction here: well under 1%.

Second, the reporting-continuity class. The question depends on credible outlets publishing a Q4 2026 ARR figure for each company. Over the past eighteen months Bloomberg, The Information, the Wall Street Journal, Reuters and the Financial Times have each published multiple dated run-rate figures for both companies, with a cadence of roughly one update every four to eight weeks per company. Two live IPO processes make disclosure more likely, not less: Anthropic's confidential draft S-1 went to the SEC on 1 June 2026 and a public filing must precede any roadshow by fifteen days, meaning audited or reviewed figures are likely to enter the public record before or around year end. The probability that no credible Q4 figure exists for either company is very low, and even then a resolver would use the most recent available figures, which already clear the bar.

Third, the trajectory class for these two firms specifically. Anthropic: roughly $9bn run rate at end-2025, $14bn in February, above $19bn in March, $30bn in April, $47bn in May, above $65bn at end-July, a sevenfold increase in seven months with no month of decline. OpenAI: above $20bn at end-2025 per CFO Sarah Friar, above $40bn by mid-August, with July alone adding more than 20% to the monthly run rate per Brockman. Every published data point in the series for both companies is an increase. There is no observation of a decline to build a contraction base rate from.

The limitations of the reference class are real and worth stating. Run rate is not a governed accounting concept; it is a company-supplied annualisation of a short window, and the two firms may compute it differently, as Axios explicitly cautioned on 17 August. The gap between Q2 recognised revenue and claimed run rate is large at OpenAI, $26.8bn annualised versus $40bn claimed, which means the headline figure is sensitive to definitional choice. There is also active analytical scrutiny of whether Anthropic's revenue should be presented gross or net, and whether annual commitments have been front-loaded into recognised revenue. So the class of "reported figures that survive an SEC review unchanged" is thinner than the class of "reported figures", and a public S-1 in September or October is a genuine restatement event.

That risk is bounded by arithmetic rather than by judgement. The combined standing figure is about $105bn. Even a punitive halving of Anthropic's number leaves $72.5bn. A definitional shift to trailing-quarter-annualised recognised revenue gives $73.2bn on Q2 data and materially more on Q4 data. Every route I can construct that a reasonable resolver would take clears $70bn. The paths to NO require either a simultaneous downward restatement at both companies of a magnitude with no precedent, or a resolver applying a definition nobody in the reporting has used. Combining a 97-99% persistence anchor with the unusually large arithmetic cushion and the guaranteed flow of IPO-driven disclosure, I settle at 99, with the interval floor at 98 to acknowledge restatement and resolution-mechanics risk rather than any doubt about the underlying business.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 34 to 32. The 18-19 August 2026 window contained one genuinely question-relevant release and several pieces of context, and on balance it removed the single most optimistic anchor in yesterday's reasoning. The decisive item is the ONS Productivity flash estimate and overview, UK: April to June 2026 and January to March 2026, published 18 August 2026 at 09:30 (I fetched this bulletin in full, plus the superseded 19 May 2026 edition, and the GOV.UK statistics landing page which confirms first-published-at 2026-08-18T09:30:01+01:00). Yesterday's forecast leaned explicitly on the 19 May release, in which the RTI/PAYE-based experimental measure showed output per hour up 2.1% year on year in Q1 2026 and 5.5% above the 2019 average, against a much weaker LFS-based headline of 0.4% year on year and 3.5% above 2019 — with ONS explicitly recommending users focus on the RTI approach. That optimistic anchor has now been overwritten by its own successor. In the 18 August print, the RTI-based flash estimate shows output per hour just 0.7% higher in the year to Q2 2026 (down from 2.1% in Q1), and minus 0.8% quarter on quarter, with the level 4.6% above the 2019 average — down from 5.5% a quarter earlier. Output per worker on the RTI basis is 1.4% higher year on year, versus 1.4% in Q1 and 1.9% in Q4 2025. ONS also quantifies the distortion from an operational error in LFS telephone collection between 3 May and 10 June 2026 (residual effects to 17 June): its best estimate is that without the issue, RTI-based output-per-hour growth would have been 0.6% rather than 0.7% in the year to Q2 2026. So the adjusted number is, if anything, slightly worse. The LFS-based measure is now outright negative: output per hour down 0.2% in the year to Q2 2026, and 2.3% above the 2019 average (down from 3.5% in Q1), with output per worker up 0.4%. Both series now converge on a picture of essentially stagnant productivity, whereas a day ago the two series told materially different stories and the ONS-preferred one was the good one.

The arithmetic matters more than the headline. Taking the RTI measure at face value, output per hour is 4.6% above the 2019 average as of Q2 2026 — roughly seven years — which compounds to about 0.64% a year. On the LFS measure, 2.3% over the same span is about 0.32% a year. Even ONS's preferred, more flattering series therefore implies a realised trend well below the roughly 1.0% underlying productivity growth the OBR assumes, and far below the 1.5%-plus that a decade average of GDP growth above 1.5% would require given demographics. The same bulletin reports whole-economy GVA up 7.1% versus the 2019 average, i.e. about 1.0% a year of actual realised GDP growth over the past seven years — a direct, ONS-sourced read on the very quantity this question is about, and one comfortably below the resolution bar. ONS also flagged that it is developing a new component-based approach to labour productivity, more closely aligned with RTI-based employment, with a methods article due in September 2026; and that initial findings from linking RTI to LFS and TLFS, which reconfirm that LFS recovery activity has reduced survey bias, will be published in autumn 2026. Those are scheduled resolution-relevant events, not evidence today, but they mean the measurement question that has been doing a lot of work in this forecast may be partially settled within two months.

The second item is the ONS Labour market overview, UK: August 2026, also released 18 August 2026 (I could not fetch the ONS bulletin page directly — provenance restrictions blocked it — so these figures come from search summaries of the ONS page and from the productivity bulletin's cross-references). Payrolled employees fell 78,000 (0.3%) in the year to June 2026 and were roughly flat on the month; the early July estimate was down 94,000 (0.3%) on the year at 30.3 million. The unemployment rate was 5.0% in April-June 2026, against 5.1% the previous quarter and 4.8% a year earlier. Around 3.9 million people are out of work and say they want a job, up 600,000 on two years ago, with 1.3 million young people not in work or full-time education. Annual regular pay growth was 3.5% and total pay 4.1% in April-June 2026, real regular pay up 0.5% on CPIH; public sector regular pay grew 6.1% against 2.8% in the private sector. This is a soft labour market, which is mostly cyclical and carries little direct information about the 2030s — but the scale of labour market detachment among the young is the kind of scarring that does show up in 2030s potential output, and the public-private pay wedge is a mild negative for aggregate measured productivity given the public sector's weaker measured output.

Third, ONS published Consumer price inflation, UK: July 2026 on 19 August 2026: CPI up 2.9% year on year (from 2.6% in June), CPIH 3.1% (from 2.8%), core CPI 2.6%, monthly CPI 0.3%, with the Ofgem cap rise of 13% on 1 July driving the housing and household services contribution and lower diesel prices offsetting through transport. The Bank's 30 July projection had CPI peaking near 3.2% in Q4 2026, so this is roughly on track and not itself a supply-side signal. It does, however, keep energy costs — a persistent structural drag on UK industrial competitiveness that the OECD flagged in its July 2026 UK survey — squarely in the picture. On 18 August the 10-year gilt yield was around 5.08%, its highest since 23 July, with 30-year around 5.7%, on a global bond selloff tied to Iran-related oil price pressure; the rise was capped by the weak labour market data. Elevated long-run real rates are a genuine 2030s headwind through the investment channel and through debt interest crowding out public capital spending.

Fourth, context just outside the window but bearing on interpretation: the ONS first quarterly estimate published 13 August 2026 put Q2 2026 GDP at plus 0.4% (after 0.6% in Q1), 1.2% higher year on year, with services up 0.5%, construction up 0.3% and production flat; June was plus 0.3%, May revised to zero, April minus 0.1%. Commentary around that release attributed nearly half of Q2 growth to information and communication and a surge in computer hardware spending — AI capex is now visible in the GDP accounts. The productivity bulletin corroborates the sectoral story: information and communication made the largest upward contribution to output per hour versus 2019 (plus 2.8 percentage points in Q1 2026), while human health and social work made the largest negative contribution (minus 0.9). This is the live bull case for the 2030s, but it is also the case that AI capex is capacity, not yet productivity, and the aggregate numbers released on 18 August show no economy-wide dividend yet.

Nothing in the window changed the fiscal or political backdrop, which is already priced: Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July 2026, John Healey is Chancellor with a "growth in every postcode" framing and fiscal control as his "first duty", and the Budget is set for 28 October 2026. There was no new OBR, Bank of England, IMF or OECD publication on 18-19 August that I could locate; the most recent relevant supply-side statement remains Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House speech. So the move is small and driven by one release. I take 2 percentage points off rather than a token 1, because the productivity flash is the flagship quarterly read on the exact variable that determines this question, it directly superseded the specific figure the prior forecast cited as its main upside anchor, and it moved that figure by 1.4 percentage points in the wrong direction while pulling the level series down 0.9 points. Two points is still a deliberately modest response to one noisy quarter.
forecasts.base_rate:
The natural reference class is UK decade averages of annual real GDP growth. On ONS data the arithmetic mean of annual growth rates was roughly 2.2% in the 1990s, 1.8% in the 2000s (dragged down by 2008-09), and about 2.0% in the 2010s (flattered by recovery from a deep output gap). The 2020s to date average roughly 1.0-1.2%, with 2026 tracking around 0.9-1.2% on outside forecasts (KPMG 0.7%, OECD 0.9%, EY 0.9%, IMF 1.0%; ONS reports Q2 2026 GDP 1.2% above a year earlier). Three of the last four completed or near-completed decades cleared 1.5%, giving a naive base rate of 60-75%. That base rate is heavily contaminated. The pre-2008 decades rested on roughly 2% trend labour productivity growth plus sustained labour force expansion from rising female participation and, from the mid-2000s, EU accession migration. Neither condition holds now. The 2010s number is an output-gap artefact: it reflects reflation of a deeply depressed economy after 2009 rather than a 2% supply-side trend, and productivity growth over that decade was roughly 0.5% a year.

A better-matched class is the post-2008 UK trend. Output per hour on the ONS RTI-based measure is 4.6% above the 2019 average as of Q2 2026 (about 0.64% a year over seven years); the LFS measure is 2.3% above (about 0.32% a year); and whole-economy GVA is 7.1% above the 2019 average, i.e. about 1.0% a year of realised GDP growth over 2019-2026. If the 2030s look like the post-2008 UK, the decade average lands near 1.0-1.2% and the question resolves NO. Against this, the ONS's own trendline analysis in the May 2026 bulletin showed Q1 2026 productivity growth in line with the 2009-2019 trend and within the 95% confidence interval around it, so the recent period is not obviously worse than the post-crisis norm — it is simply that the post-crisis norm is well below what the question requires.

A third class is decadal growth forecasts for advanced economies made three to four years ahead of the decade start. These have historically been poorly calibrated in both directions: the 2010s were widely under-forecast at the trough of the crisis, the 2020s were over-forecast pre-COVID, and long-horizon OBR and Bank potential-growth assumptions have repeatedly been revised down over the past fifteen years. The revision asymmetry is real: the OBR has cut its trend productivity assumption several times and has essentially never raised it materially. That asymmetry argues for weighting the pessimistic tail more heavily than a symmetric distribution around a 1.2% central case would.

The demographic accounting is the tightest constraint. The ONS 2024-based National Population Projections (published 28 April 2026) put the working-age population up 1.5 million, or 3.4%, between mid-2024 and mid-2034 — about 0.34% a year — and ONS expects natural change to turn negative in the mid-2030s, so that beyond 2035 population growth is entirely migration-dependent under current assumptions. With hours per worker on a mild downward trend and the employment rate at best flat given ageing, labour input plausibly contributes 0.0 to 0.4 percentage points a year in the 2030s. To average above 1.5% you therefore need trend productivity growth of roughly 1.1-1.5% a year sustained for a decade — comfortably above the OBR's ~1.0% assumption and roughly double the realised post-2019 rate on ONS's preferred measure.

Two mechanical considerations push up. First, an output-gap effect: if the UK has a recession in the late 2020s, the 2030s decade average is mechanically boosted by recovery growth, exactly as the 2010s were. Given the current soft labour market (unemployment 5.0%, payrolled employees down 78,000 on the year), that path is far from remote. Second, ONS revisions have systematically been upward for post-pandemic UK GDP, and the question resolves on ONS-reported figures, so the reported decade average is more likely to be revised up than down relative to the first estimates.

Blending: a base-rate-consistent central case for 2030s average annual growth is around 1.2%, with a wide distribution — call it a standard deviation of 0.45-0.55 percentage points across scenarios, with a fat right tail from AI diffusion and a fat left tail from fiscal and energy-cost drag. That places P(mean > 1.5%) at roughly 27-33%. Adding a small allowance for AI optionality and for the recession-recovery mechanic, and subtracting for the systematic downward-revision asymmetry in UK potential-growth estimates, gives 32%.
